messages.body_plain:
I just wanted to check in and see if anything has come about in the past two years to model repeated counts with distance and time removal? I have a similar dataset as Amy and I'm curious what she ended up doing. I've been using pcountopen (because I am looking at the effects of harvesting between years), but I started playing around with gdistsamp yesterday.

5 study areas with 10-40 point count stations each
Each point count was sampled 3 times in a breeding season (10-min counts split into five 2-minute intervals and five distance bins)
Each point count was sampled at least one year pre-harvest and at least one year post-harvest
Harvests occurred in different calendar years so I use a years-since-harvest effect instead of year. I have some sites with one or two years of pre-harvest data and two or three years of post-harvest data. To handle that, I am only using data from the season immediately preceding the harvest and then one-year since harvest. I have a separate analysis for post-harvest only data so that I can take advantage of more of the data that I collected. For that I used a stacked pcount approach.

With the gdistsamp I ran post-harvest data and got results that make sense. I am going to try stacking the pre- and post-harvest data and adding a harvest variable.

I want to look at change in songbird abundance pre- vs post-harvest and if that change in abundance is correlated to a particular vegetation or topographical variable (aspect, slope position, basal area, etc.)

Thanks!
Gretchen

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] why does scaling covariate change occupancy estimate?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] why does scaling covariate change occupancy estimate?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

This isn’t a problem in general, but you are using very extreme covariate values. When a covariate takes on such extreme values, it causes numerical problems on the logit scale, making it hard for the optimizer to find the MLEs. For example, if you fiddle around with this code you will see how sensitive the response is to small changes in beta1:
beta0 <- -1
beta1 <- 0.01
x <- 1e6*rnorm(100)      # covariate with extreme values
plogis(beta0 + beta1*x)

The solution is to avoid extreme covariate values by using a z-transformation or similar. This is true for most GLM-type models, not just the models in unmarked.

Richard
​

I understand that scaling/centering the covariate may affect the interpretation of the coefficient on the covariate, but that coefficient is not of direct interest to me -- I am including the covariate only to obtain better estimates of occupancy.
>
> To illustrate, consider the following example with a fake covariate. For small covariate values, the occupancy estimate comes out close to 1. For 'large' covariate values, e.g. 10^5, the occupancy estimate comes out close to 0.5.

messages.body_plain:
Correct. You want the data exactly like the data in your model. So if the data in your model is scaled, then you want the data in your new data to be scaled (using the same mean and standard deviation as your original data). If you just want to predict at the mean of scaled covariates, then you can just set the covariates equal to zero. If you want to predict across the whole range of covariate values you observed, then you can do a sequence from the minimum scaled covariate value to the maximum scaled covariate value (in which case you probably want to use the function expand.grid() instead of data.frame().)

messages.subject: occuFP example script (occupancy with false positives)
messages.subject_clean: occuFP example script (occupancy with false positives)
messages.body_plain:
hi all,
 the example code in the help file for occuFP has been deficient for a long time so I spent some time this week writing an example script that shows how to simulate and package up data and how to fit different models.  I will clean this up during the summer and make it part of the help file for occuFP for the next release (not until January probably). But for now, here is the script which shows, in succession, how to simulate and fit a model for:

 1. a mix of ordinary occupancy data (no false positives) and some data contaminated with false positives

 2. data which are all contaminated with false positives

 3. occupancy data with no false positives + some contaminated with false positives + some "known true positive" data

 For more detail on what this all means see the help file for occuFP (thanks to David Miller from years ago) as well as read his paper Miller et al. (2011) cited in the help file.

regards,
andy

# Read the help file
# Here we simulate some data and we fit a model of type 2 which has some ordinary occupancy data NOT
# subject to false positives and also some that are subject to false positives... we assume a total of
# K=7 sample intervals of which the first 2 are assumed to be subject to no false positives.
# We simulate a habitat covariate and we suppose p varies between the first 2 samples and the last
# 5 which we code with a dummy variable for inputting to the scrFrame
# Sites, reps, and K1 = number of ordinary occupancy reps
M = 200
K = 7
K1= 2
# occupancy model
habitat<- rnorm(M)
alpha0<- 0
alpha1<- 1
psi<- plogis( alpha0 + alpha1*habitat)
z<- rbinom(M, 1, psi)
# Detection parameters and data simulation
y = matrix(0,M,K)
p = c(0.7, 0.5)  # method 2 will have a lower p
fp = 0.05
for(i in 1:M){
# Normal occupancy data
 y[i,1:2]<- rbinom(1, 1, p[1]*z[i])
# False-positives mixed in
 y[i,3:7]<- rbinom(5, 1, p[2]*z[i] + fp*(1-z[i]) )
}

## type is a vector with the number of each data type 1, 2, 3 (see help file). In this case, 2 sites are of type 1
## (ordinary occupancy) and 5 sites are of type 2 (contaminated with false positives) and there are no type 3 sites
## These are assumed to be in the corresponding columns of the encounter data matrix. i.e., rows 1-2 are type 1, etc..
type<- c(2, 5, 0)
# one site covariate which is binary (2 groups of sites) and 1 obs covariate which is binary "method"
occ <- matrix(c(rep(0,M*(K-K1)),rep(1,M*K1)),M,K)
siteCovs <- data.frame(habitat = habitat)
obsCovs <- list(METH = occ)
library(unmarked)
umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y,siteCovs = siteCovs, obsCovs = obsCovs, type = type)
m1 <- occuFP(detformula = ~ METH, FPformula = ~1,
             stateformula = ~ habitat, data = umf1)
m1

# Standard unmarked summary functions work with the occuFP models:
head(predict(m1, type = 'fp') )
coef(m1)
confint(m1, type = 'det')

#
# Next we consider a situation where we don't have any perfect occupancy data, only data subject to
# false positives (type 2 data), but the first 2 occasions have a different p from the last 5
# Its important to use starting values for the false positive parameter in this model to
# avoid finding the wrong maximum of the likelihood (see below)
#
M = 200
K = 7
K1= 2
habitat<- rnorm(M)
alpha0<- 0
alpha1<- 1
psi<- plogis( alpha0 + alpha1*habitat)
z<- rbinom(M, 1, psi)
y = matrix(0,M,K)
p = c(0.7, 0.5)  # method 2 will have a lower p
fp = 0.05
# simulate the data. Note here both chunks of data are simulated with the false positives
for(i in 1:M){
# Normal occupancy data
 y[i,1:2]<- rbinom(2, 1, p[1]*z[i] + fp*(1-z[i]) )
# False-positives mixed in
 y[i,3:7]<- rbinom(5, 1, p[2]*z[i] + fp*(1-z[i]) )
}

# type indicates all 7 occasions correspond to false positives data
type<- c(0, 7, 0)

# one site covariate which is binary (2 groups of sites) and 1 obs covariate which is binary "method"
occ <- matrix(c(rep(0,M*(K-K1)),rep(1,M*K1)),M,K)
siteCovs <- data.frame(habitat = habitat)
obsCovs <- list(METH = occ)
umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y,siteCovs = siteCovs, obsCovs = obsCovs, type = type)
# starting values are important here or else MLE finds the wrong mode!
m2 <- occuFP(detformula = ~ METH,       FPformula = ~1,
             stateformula = ~ habitat,  data = umf1, starts=c(0,0,0,0, -1) )
m2

#
# now here we will consider some type 3 observations which we will assume exist as column 7 of the
# encounter history data. Remember these take on values 0 not detected, 1 = detected but uncertain, 2 = confirmed occupied
#

M = 200
K = 7
K1= 2
habitat<- rnorm(M)
alpha0<- 0
alpha1<- 1
psi<- plogis( alpha0 + alpha1*habitat)
z<- rbinom(M, 1, psi)
y = matrix(0,M,K)
p = c(0.7, 0.5)  # method 2 will have a lower p
b<- 0.5  # probability that a false positive is determined to be certain
fp = 0.05
# simulate the data.
for(i in 1:M){
# Normal occupancy data
 y[i,1:2]<- rbinom(2, 1, p[1]*z[i]   )
# False-positives mixed in
 y[i,3:6]<- rbinom(4, 1, p[2]*z[i] + fp*(1-z[i]) )
 # Type 3 observations are occupancy data contaminated with false positives but then we identify some of them as true
 y[i, 7]<- rbinom(1, 1, p[2]*z[i] + fp*(1-z[i]) )
}
  true.positives<- z==1 & y[,7]==1
  confirmed<- (rbinom(M, 1, b) ==1)   & true.positives
  y[confirmed, 7]<- 2

# type indicates all 7 occasions correspond to false positives data
type<- c(2, 4, 1)

# One site covariate which is binary (2 groups of sites) and 1 obs covariate which is binary "method"
occ <- matrix(c(rep(0,M*(K-K1)),rep(1,M*K1)),M,K)
siteCovs <- data.frame(habitat = habitat)
obsCovs <- list(METH = occ)
umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y,siteCovs = siteCovs, obsCovs = obsCovs, type = type)
# starting values are important here or else MLE finds the wrong mode!  Note: last parameter in this model is "Pcertain"
m3 <- occuFP(detformula = ~ METH,       FPformula = ~1,  Bformula = ~1,
             stateformula = ~ habitat,  data = umf1, starts=c(0,0,0,0, -1, 0) )
m3
# Potentially the parameter b might also depend on covariates, so we accommodate that here.

m3b <- occuFP(detformula = ~ METH,       FPformula = ~1,  Bformula = ~ habitat,
             stateformula = ~ habitat,  data = umf1, starts=c(0,0,0,0, -1, 0,0) )
m3b

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to run a very basic occupancy model in unmarked using occu(). I imported three detection matrices (from camtrapR) in identical formats, and ran the same bare-bones model on each data set just to get occupancy and detection probabilities:

model <- occu(~1 ~1, data = grid)

The model ran for two of the three datasets without a problem, but the third gave the error:

Error: Hessian is singular.  Try providing starting values or using fewer covariates.

I have tried providing starting values by adding "starts = c(0,0)" (and a couple of different values just to test), and there are no covariates. Any other ideas about what might cause this error?

Below is some more info on the data set that is not working. There are a lot more 0 observations—could that be the issue? All three data sets have many NA observations.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kaitlyn,

the issue with that dataset is that the species was detected at all sits which means occupancy is 1. In this case the model can't estimate parameters and there really is no need for an occupancy model. If I interpret your summary right the number of observations are really large indicating that in some cases you had almost 1000 sampling occasions. Even with camera traps and a one-day sampling period that would require over 2.5 years of sampling which would certainly violate any closure assumption. In any case you might want to reduce your sampling periods to 5 or 7 days.

Deepening on your dataset and research questions you might also want to analyze the three datasets in a single model with some parameters shared.

Best,

Mathias

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] VIF and UMF
messages.body_plain:
Hi Frederic,

if you want to assess multicollinearity among different predictors with the variance inflation factor (VIF), you can just run a classic linear regression with any random response variable as a function of the predictors of interest. Specifically, to estimate the VIF of a given variable, you 1) regress the variable against the remaining predictors, 2) extract the R^2 of the regression, and then, 3)  VIF = 1/(1 - R^2).

If you're using the vif( ) function in the car package, you can see this using the cement data set:

library(car)

data(cement, package = "AICcmodavg")

head(cement)

##run model with y as response

m1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = cement)

##extract VIF

vif(m1)

##create bogus variable

cement$bogus <- lm(bogus ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = cement)
vif(m2)

It is straightforward to do this for predictors on occupancy. For predictors on detection probability, you'll need to "unfold" the data so that each predictor is in its own column, before estimating VIF.

Hope it helps,

Marc

in order for it to get the VIF, you need to run the regressions with lm( ), not occu( ). For instance, to determine the VIF for the predictors div_pente, Surf_AO, and  altitude, which are fit on occupancy in your case, then just do:

m1 <- lm(bogusResponse ~  div_pente + Surf_AO + altitude,

data = aClassicDataFrame)

vif(m1)

Here, bogusResponse is a (random) numeric variable that must appear somewhere in your classic R data.frame, not UMF.

Marc

messages.subject: Spatial Replication and Abundance Predictions
messages.subject_clean: Spatial Replication and Abundance Predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Frequent reader, first time poster here.

Hopefully this will be a quick and easy question to answer, however I have been unable to find an answer through related papers or searching this group.

I am estimating abundance of a fish, using the unmarked function pcount(). My study design was as follows: Within each of 2 streams I sampled several 120m stream reaches (the site level), and then 12 independent 10m^2 plots within each reach (the observational level). I am using these plots as spatial replicates in place of temporal replicates typically used in these models. Essentially, instead of re-sampling X number of times I sampled 12 plots within the same site as my replicates. So I have a count associated with each replicate of each site.

I modeled with my covariates for detection and abundance and came up with my fitted models. Using either predict() or ranef() I get a matrix which includes a column related to my predictions. For example ranef produces:

 Mean                   Mode 2.5% 97.5%
 [1,]  5.35481832    5    3     8
 [2,] 22.13031890   22   17    28
 [3,] 25.37614331   26   20    29
 [4,]  3.53496729    3    1     6
 [5,]  0.00203653    0    0     0
 [6,]  9.15349140    9    6    12
 [7,] 15.54310502   15   12    20
 [8,] 15.85494164   16   12    21
 [9,]  7.79657345    7    5    12
[10,]  5.92160048    6    3     9

I would interpret the Mean column here as representing the predicted abundance for a site when using the typical temporal replication template.

My question is: Would I be correct in interpreting these results in that the Mean column represents the predicted abundance for the area corresponding to one plot (or replicate), not the combination of all 12 plot areas (total area sampled in a site) given the spatial replication template. So with a plot area of 10m^2 the site listed as 1 would have an average predicted density of 0.53 fish/m^2 not 0.046 fish/m^2 if it is a prediction for the total area sampled (120m^2).

I do have R code for all of the modeling process, but I am hopeful that this brief description of my study design will be sufficient to answer the question.

Thanks,

Davy Black

Hi Davy,

Yep, these are site-specific values and not summaries across the entire set of sites (although those summaries could be derived).

For a more thorough treatment, you might look at some of the references associated with ranef-methods in the package's reference manual, but: informally, values returned by ranef might be thought of as estimates of the state variable (abundance, occupancy, etc.) at that particular site/time. The predict function returns predictions.

Cheers,

John
